Oil news graph / local collection audit

What the interrupted news collection can support

Offline exploratory analysis of the interrupted multilingual collection. The original downloader, raw files, classifier outputs and assembled datasets were read without modification. All counts below come from this machine; the older Russian-only notebook and the non-news EDA remain separate.

1. Findings that change the research plan

  1. The corpus is substantial but incomplete: 716,710 of 3,870,772 selected rows have a saved fetch attempt (18.5%). The missing portion is unobserved collection work, not evidence that no news occurred.
  2. The US index contains 2,074,729 rows but only 10,781 assembled articles, dated 2026-03-30–2026-10-31. Its marked duplicate fraction is 57.6%. This snapshot cannot support a 2015–2022 US full-text training set.
  3. Exact repeated text is material: 30,918 rows are marked as local duplicates; full-corpus hashing finds 34,717 redundant rows and 3,743 text clusters spanning multiple source countries. Syndication and overlapping collections can inflate counts and graph centrality.
  4. Dates need repair: 17 rows have an out-of-range or explicitly unreliable resolved date; 1 fall after the collection end. URL-derived dates are evidence to inspect, not ground truth.
  5. All 460,460 saved rows contain only publication-day resolution for the EDA cutoff
  6. The saved model uses identical keep and drop thresholds (0.503766). This creates a binary filter, with 0 borderline decisions in the saved scores. Its current-corpus precision cannot be verified without local gold labels.
  7. The broad title screens flag 1,098 possible inventory-reporting stories. These require leakage review before they become predictors; title keyword matches are not validated event labels.

2. Collection accounting and what remains unfinished

Each country is a Media Cloud source collection. A US-source story can describe Saudi Arabia; a Saudi-source story can discuss US inventories. Four regions use full-stream queries while most use recall terms, so retention rates have different denominators. Packed multi-month filenames are expanded to calendar months; file counts are not month counts. Metadata counts include existing snapshots, even when a stage was interrupted.

3. Fetch failures and selection bias

The failure audit deduplicates retries by story ID and takes the latest fetched_at, matching the downloader's read policy. The extraction count precedes assembly cleaning. Failed attempts and successfully extracted texts excluded as templates are different outcomes. Recent-first processing concentrates partial corpora near the collection end; a successful live fetch in 2026 is also not proof that the recovered text is the original historical version.

4. Classifier scores, languages and representativeness

The saved multilingual-e5-base title model was trained on 20,068 examples. Its metadata reports PR-AUC 0.973, language-macro PR-AUC 0.959, stratum-weighted PR-AUC 0.532, and temporal PR-AUC 0.970. The gap between unweighted and weighted metrics matters. These are historical model-development metrics, not a new validation of this corpus. Score thresholds should not be interpreted as calibrated event probabilities. No encoder or paid labeler was run for this EDA.

6. Text quality, exact repeats and date errors

Character counts are language-neutral diagnostics; whitespace word counts are not comparable across all scripts. The basic screen requires a nonempty title, a normalized text hash, 300–100,000 characters, a resolved date within 2015-01-01–2026-10-31, and date_source other than unreliable. It leaves 460,339 rows before global text deduplication. These thresholds are transparent EDA choices, not learned quality labels.

Content screens flag 90 rows: recognizable consent/access messages in the first 600 characters, or one text used at least ten times under at least five distinct titles over more than 30 days. These rows are excluded from the inspection-ready screen, pending manual review. A concrete case is the iDNES advertising-consent text surviving on many subdomains: per-host template removal misses a template spread across subdomains. The largest US clusters, in contrast, show wire-service syndication across dozens of stations.

7. Physical themes, direct inventory reports and graph anchors

The title dictionaries cover several observed languages and allow overlap. They are useful for finding review examples, not comparing countries' true event prevalence. Matched production, refining, pipeline, outage, weather and shipping themes suggest event candidates. Generic price commentary and reporting of the EIA/API result should be reviewed separately. The event screen excludes inventory-reporting matches but has neither measured precision nor measured recall.

Company and location title mentions provide initial linking candidates. Building the graph still requires entity disambiguation, facility IDs, event time, source publication time, capacity units, direction and duration. Missing a title keyword is not evidence that an article lacks a relevant entity in its body.

8. EIA release alignment and historical feasibility

For exploratory alignment only, an article is assigned to the first observed Myfxbook EIA release strictly after its normalized publication day. This excludes all same-day stories because intraday availability cannot be established. The first window has no known start; missing calendar releases create longer windows. Windows other than seven days are flagged and excluded from the descriptive correlation screen. This is conservative by publication date but does not certify that the text, extraction version, or corrected timestamp was known at the historical cutoff.

The target calendar inherits the existing Myfxbook caveats: missing weeks in 2022 and 2023, and an ambiguous delayed publication in June 2022. No missing releases or consensus values were fabricated. The target and API estimates are used as outcomes/context, not features extracted from the article text.

The weekly panel retains indexed, selected, attempted and assembled counts. observed_text_count is missing when no texts were attempted. An attempted fraction of at least 80% is a coverage sensitivity screen, not a claim of completeness. Even fully attempted selections remain conditioned on the query, classifier and fetch success.

Pipeline throughput is grouped by the original index publication date; assembled content is grouped by the resolved publication date. Corrections can move stories between windows, so stage ratios are diagnostics rather than exact same-window recovery probabilities. Large date disagreements should be reviewed before modeling.

9. News counts versus inventory surprise: descriptive screen

Spearman correlations below use assembled counts in seven-day windows with at least 30 observations, once for all attempted windows and once for windows with at least 80% of selected stories attempted. Benjamini–Hochberg p-values adjust across the complete displayed family. Counts still reflect archive and recovery bias, duplicates and source mix. This is an exploratory association, not a predictive test or evidence of incremental value over API. The reviewed non-news baseline already shows that API minus consensus is a strong comparator.

Measured result: 0 of 50 country/coverage comparisons pass a 5% false-discovery threshold. This screen provides no convincing evidence that raw publication counts predict the inventory surprise.

10. Concrete next steps for the graph dataset

  1. Repair the date resolver against the anomalies above, retaining original and corrected fields plus the reason. Reassemble only after testing those cases.
  2. Use the stage and monthly tables to backfill missing historical texts, prioritizing US training years and publisher strata with large remaining selected counts. Do not treat partial months as zero events.
  3. Annotate the stratified review sample for oil relevance, physical event type, text quality and date validity. It is enriched for difficult cases and is not a probability sample for estimating corpus-wide precision.
  4. Collapse exact text into one document node, keep publisher/URL/country provenance as edges, and split duplicate groups together during evaluation. Review repeated-title variants before adding near-duplicate clustering.
  5. Extract event location independently of source country. Link facilities and companies to the infrastructure tables with explicit confidence and unresolved cases.
  6. Fix a prediction timestamp and collect genuine publication/availability evidence. Validate incremental performance over consensus, API and pre-release fundamentals with temporal evaluation after coverage and leakage audits pass.

Manual review file: eda/data/derived/news/review_sample.csv, 366 rows. Human label fields are deliberately blank. The compact article audit includes excerpts and flags; the original full texts remain in the source datasets.

11. Reproduction, provenance and checks

Run MPLCONFIGDIR=/tmp/oil-news-matplotlib .venv/bin/python eda/news_eda.py from the repository root. Open eda/notebooks/08_news_corpus.ipynb for the executed walkthrough. The analyzer reads one country at a time, uses no network, does not retrain the classifier, and writes only derived EDA tables and this report. Seed: 6107. Tables are Parquet plus a CSV review sample; the HTML embeds its figures and can be shared as a single file.
